title: Linked Lists, Stacks, Queues & Pointer Patterns
summary: Quick revision notes on singly and doubly linked lists, stacks, queues, deques, the monotonic stack and fast/slow pointers, with the cost of each common operation and the mistakes that cost marks in interviews.

chapters.title: Linear Structures: The Mental Model
points: Singly linked list: each node holds value + next; only head is known, so access by index is O(n)
Doubly linked list: node adds prev, so delete-given-node and tail removal are O(1) at the cost of one extra pointer per node
Stack = LIFO (push/pop/peek at one end); queue = FIFO (enqueue at back, dequeue at front); deque = O(1) at both ends
Array vs linked list: array gives O(1) index and cache-friendly scans; list gives O(1) insert/delete once you hold the node
Interview Point: Why is deleting a given node O(1) in a doubly list but O(n) in a singly list? When would you pick a list over a dynamic array?

chapters.title: Linked List Operations and Costs
points: Insert at head O(1); insert at tail O(1) only with a tail pointer, else O(n)
Search by value O(n); delete by value O(n) to find, O(1) to unlink
Traverse with cur = head; while cur: cur = cur.next, and keep prev to unlink a node
Use a dummy (sentinel) head node to remove special cases when inserting or deleting the first node
Reverse a list iteratively: save nxt = cur.next, set cur.next = prev, advance prev = cur, cur = nxt; O(n) time, O(1) space
Interview Point: How do you reverse a singly list in place? Why use a dummy head? What is the cost of appending without a tail pointer?

chapters.title: Stacks and Queues in Practice
points: Stack in Python is a list: append() to push, pop() to pop, [-1] to peek; all O(1) amortized
Queue should be collections.deque: append() to enqueue, popleft() to dequeue in O(1)
Stack use: balanced brackets, undo, DFS, expression evaluation; queue use: BFS, task scheduling, buffering
Deque ops: append, appendleft, pop, popleft all O(1); supports sliding-window maximum
Interview Point: How do you implement a queue with two stacks and what is the amortized cost? Why is list.pop(0) a bad dequeue? Which structure does BFS use versus DFS?

chapters.title: Monotonic Stack
points: Monotonic stack keeps elements in sorted order (increasing or decreasing); pop while the top violates the order, then push
Next greater element: scan left to right, keep a decreasing stack of indices; when a[i] > a[top], pop and set answer[top] = a[i]
Each element is pushed and popped at most once, so the whole pass is O(n) despite the inner while loop
Store indices, not values, when you need distances (daily temperatures) or widths (largest rectangle in histogram)
Interview Point: Why is a nested while loop here still O(n)? Should the stack hold values or indices, and when? How would you find the next smaller element?

chapters.title: Fast and Slow Pointers
points: Two pointers: slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2 steps per iteration; O(n) time, O(1) space
Cycle detection (Floyd): if slow == fast at some point, a cycle exists; if fast or fast.next is None, there is none
Middle of a list: when fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle; for even length it lands on the second middle
Cycle start: after meeting, reset one pointer to head and move both 1 step; they meet at the cycle entrance
Mistake: loop condition while fast and fast.next, else fast.next.next raises a null error
Interview Point: Why must fast and slow meet inside a cycle? How do you find the cycle's start node? How do you get the first middle of an even-length list?

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet: Lists, Stacks, Queues
points: Costs: array index O(1), list index O(n), list head insert O(1), doubly delete-given-node O(1), deque both ends O(1)
Stack = list append/pop; queue = deque append/popleft; never list.pop(0)
Linked list tricks: dummy head, prev pointer when unlinking, save next before rewiring, tail pointer for O(1) append
Monotonic stack: store indices, pop while violated, O(n) overall; decreasing stack gives next greater
Fast/slow: while fast and fast.next; meet means cycle; reset to head to find the entrance
Common mistakes: losing the rest of the list by overwriting next first, off-by-one on null checks, popping an empty stack
